                    ### Question
                    An 80-year-old man is admitted with a sudden picture of aphasia and right hemiparesis. As background highlights, hypertension, well controlled diet and cognitive impairment in the last year under study by his neurologist. Emergency cranial CT demonstrates a left frontal lobar hematoma without contrast enhancement. What is the most likely cause of the hematoma?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Arteriovenous malformation masked by the acute hematoma.
opb. Chronic arterial hypertension.
opc. Vasculitis isolated from the nervous system.
opd. Brain tumor.
ope. Amyloid cerebral angiopathy (congophilic angiopathy).

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely cause of the hematoma in the 80-year-old man with aphasia and right hemiparesis is chronic arterial hypertension. Chronic arterial hypertension can lead to weakening of blood vessel walls, increasing the risk of hemorrhage, which aligns with the findings of a left frontal lobar hematoma on cranial CT. The presence of amyloid cerebral angiopathy may also contribute to vessel fragility and hemorrhage risk, but in this case, chronic arterial hypertension is the more likely primary cause.
